prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Mother, Things, The

outputs.L1:
Mother, the root of this little yellow flower  
Among the stones tastes of quinine.  
Things are strange today upon the cliff. The sun shines so brightly,  
And the grasshopper works so hard  
At his sewing machine. Here is one on my hand, Mother—look;  
I lie so still. There is one on your book.  

But I have something stranger still to tell. So leave  
Your book to the grasshopper, Mother dear—  
Like a green knight in a dazzling marketplace—  
And listen now. Can you hear what I hear  
Far out? Now and then the foam curls there  
And stretches out a white arm like a girl’s.  

Fishes and gulls ring no bells. There cannot be  
A chapel or church between here and Devon,  
With fishes or gulls ringing its bell—hark!—  
Somewhere under the sea or up in heaven.  

“It is the bell, my son, out in the bay,  
On the buoy. It does sound sweet today.”  

Sweeter I have never heard, Mother—no, not in all Wales.  
I should like to be lying beneath that foam,  
Dead, yet still able to hear the bell,  
And certain that you would often come  
And rest, listening happily.  
I should be happy if that could be.
outputs.L2:
Mother, this small yellow blossom growing between the rocks has a root that tastes bitter, like quinine.

Everything feels unusual on the cliff today. The sunlight is intensely bright, and the grasshopper is rasping away as though it were busy at a sewing machine. Look, mother—there is one sitting on my hand. I am keeping perfectly still. And there is another on your book.

But I have something even stranger to tell you, so put your book aside for the grasshopper, dear mother—he looks like a little green knight in a glittering marketplace—and listen to me. Do you hear the sound I hear, far away? Every so often the foam out there curls and reaches out a pale arm, almost like a girl’s.

Fish and seagulls do not ring bells. There cannot be any chapel or church between this place and Devon where fish or gulls are ringing one—listen! It must be somewhere beneath the sea, or else up in the sky.

“That is the bell, my son,” you say, “the one on the buoy out in the bay. It sounds especially lovely today.”

Mother, I have never heard anything sweeter—not anywhere in Wales. I think I would like to be lying beneath that foam, dead, yet still able to hear that bell, and to know that you would come often to sit there and listen peacefully.

If that were possible, I would be content.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a vivid moment shared between a child and the child’s mother on a cliff above the sea. The speaker notices strange, bright, and memorable details in the landscape: a yellow flower growing on the cliff, the intense sunlight, and grasshoppers moving through the grass. These images make the scene feel alive and unusually clear, as if the child is experiencing the world with heightened awareness.

While standing there, the child hears a mysterious sound coming from far out at sea. It seems like a bell, distant and beautiful, carrying across the water. The child does not immediately understand where it comes from, and this makes the sound feel almost magical. The mother then explains that it is the bell on a buoy in the bay, ringing as the buoy moves with the waves.

Even after learning its ordinary source, the child finds the bell’s sound exceptionally sweet. The sound becomes more than just a warning bell or a feature of the seascape; it enters the child’s imagination. The child imagines hearing it from beneath the sea, as though the sound could continue even in a hidden, underwater world.

In this way, the poem connects the beauty of the bell with deeper thoughts about death, peace, and comfort. The child’s imagination turns toward the idea of being under the sea, but the thought is not frightening. Instead, it is calm and strangely beautiful because the bell would still be heard, and the mother would still somehow be present. The poem therefore blends vivid natural details with a child’s tender reflections on death, suggesting that love and peace can continue beyond fear.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a child’s mysterious and deeply sensory experience on a cliff by the sea. Through vivid images of the natural world—the sound of the buoy’s bell, the movement of the waves, the height of the cliff, and the presence of the surrounding air and water—the poem creates an atmosphere that is both beautiful and unsettling. The child does not simply observe the landscape; he feels drawn into it, as if the sea and its sounds are speaking directly to him. This makes the setting seem almost magical, filled with meanings that go beyond ordinary reality.

At the center of the poem is the tender dialogue between the child and his mother. Their conversation reveals the child’s unusual thoughts about death, memory, and comfort. Rather than imagining death as something frightening, the child connects it with beauty, music, and the continuing love of his mother. He imagines a peaceful afterlife in which the sound of the buoy’s bell would remain with him, gently reminding him of the world he has left behind and of the mother who loves him. In this way, the bell becomes more than a simple object in the sea. It becomes a symbol of reassurance, continuity, and emotional connection.

The poem is powerful because it blends innocence with deep emotional intensity. The child’s thoughts are strange, but they are also moving, because they show his desire to be remembered and comforted even after death. His imagination brings together the sea, the bell, his mother, and the idea of an afterlife into one vision of peace. The natural imagery helps express feelings that are difficult to state directly: longing, fear, love, and the wish for a beautiful form of rest. Ultimately, the poem reveals how a child’s imagination transforms death into something gentle and meaningful, with the buoy’s bell sounding like a promise that love and memory will continue.
outputs.L5:
**The Things a Mother Keeps**

A mother keeps many things: small drawings on the fridge, tiny shoes that no longer fit, birthday cards, and memories hidden in the quiet corners of her heart. The world may see these as ordinary things, but to a mother, they are pieces of a life she has loved, protected, and watched grow.

The love of a mother is often found in simple moments: a warm meal, a gentle voice, a hand held during fear, or a smile that says everything will be okay. She may not always speak of her sacrifices, but they live in the things she does every day.

The greatest things a mother gives are not always seen. They are patience, strength, kindness, and hope. These gifts remain with her children long after they have grown, reminding them that love is not only something spoken—it is something lived.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Edward Thomas, beginning with a child speaking to his mother on a sunny cliff, mentioning a yellow flower root that tastes of quinine, grasshoppers, sea foam, gulls, Devon, Wales, and a bell buoy in the bay.
counterfactuals.output:
“Mother, what is this yellow flower-root  
That tastes of quinine, bitter in the sun?”  
The child spat, laughing, where the short grass stood  
Warm on the cliff, and grasshoppers begun  
Their little dry machinery at our feet.

Below, the sea foam travelled, fold on fold,  
And gulls went crying down the empty air;  
Far off, the Devon headlands, blue and old,  
Looked back to Wales, as if remembering there  
Some road the water never would complete.

A bell buoy in the bay said one dull word,  
Again, again, through glitter and through haze;  
And every time it spoke the bright day stirred,  
Then settled deeper into summer’s maze,  
Where nothing seemed to end, or to have been.

“Mother,” he said, and held the root once more,  
“The flower is sweet, but all its heart is gall.”  
She smiled, and watched the light along the shore,  
The gulls, the foam, the buoy’s far patient call—  
And heard, past noon, how quiet grief can sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholy pastoral dialogue between a child and his mother by the sea, where the child hears a mysterious bell and imagines lying dead under the foam while his mother visits and listens.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bell Beneath the Foam**

**Child.**  
Mother, the sheep are folded on the hill,  
and every gull is gone.  
Why does the sea keep calling still,  
when all the day is done?

**Mother.**  
It is the tide among the stones,  
the wind along the shore;  
it gathers up the earth’s old moans  
and brings them to our door.

**Child.**  
No, mother, no—it is a bell.  
I hear it clear and low,  
as if some little chapel fell  
a hundred years ago.

It rings beneath the green sea-floor,  
beneath the drifting foam;  
perhaps it calls the drowned ashore,  
perhaps it calls me home.

**Mother.**  
Hush, child, and lean against my knee;  
the night comes cold and deep.  
No bell can sound beneath the sea—  
it is the waves asleep.

**Child.**  
If I were sleeping there, instead,  
where pale weed round me clings,  
and shells were pillows for my head,  
would I hear when it rings?

If I lay still below the foam,  
with sand upon my eyes,  
would you come walking out from home  
under the empty skies?

**Mother.**  
I’d come at dusk, when lambs are still,  
and dew is on the grass;  
I’d leave the path beside the hill  
and watch the gray waves pass.

**Child.**  
And would you listen, mother dear,  
where the long ripples run,  
to hear the bell ring faint and clear  
far under sea and sun?

**Mother.**  
I’d listen till the stars grew dim,  
till dawn unlatched the day;  
and if the bell should call to him,  
I’d kneel beside the bay.

**Child.**  
Then do not weep if I should keep  
a bed you cannot see;  
the sea has little bells for sleep,  
and one may ring for me.

**Mother.**  
O child, my child, the pasture fades,  
the ewes cry on the lea;  
come home before the darkness wades  
too deeply through the sea.

**Child.**  
I come—but still the bell goes on,  
below the foam, below;  
it sounds as lonely as the dawn  
that no one lives to know.

**Mother.**  
Then let it ring for ships astray,  
for bones the waters hide;  
but not for you, my child—not today.  
Walk close here at my side.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical early-20th-century English poem about a mother and son on a cliff, with vivid natural imagery, a grasshopper like a sewing machine, and the sound of a buoy bell mistaken for something supernatural.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bell in the Sea-Mist**

Upon the cliff at evening-tide  
The mother and the child stood near,  
Where thrift and thyme grew side by side  
And gulls went crying, keen and clear.  

Below, the long sea shouldered foam,  
Green glass, grey steel, and sudden white;  
The west was like a burning home  
Behind the fallen doors of light.  

A grasshopper in withered grass,  
Close-hidden by the rabbit-run,  
Ticked like a small sewing-machine  
Mending the silence of the sun.  

The boy leaned out; his hair was blown  
About his face like barley pale.  
He watched the great waves grind the stone,  
And ships grow ghostly through the veil.  

Then, far beyond the wrack and roar,  
Where dusk had dimmed the harbour’s bound,  
There came from off the unseen shore  
A hollow, slow, unearthly sound.  

“Mother,” he whispered, drawing back,  
“Is that the church beneath the sea?  
Or dead men tolling in the black  
For sailors drowned and lost to thee?”  

She held his hand, though in her breast  
Old tales awoke with bat-like wings:  
Of bells that rang and souls unblest,  
And mermaids combing dead men’s rings.  

Yet softly then she bent her head,  
And smiled as mothers smile at fear:  
“Nay, child; the buoy bell rings,” she said,  
“To warn the boats when fog is near.”  

But still across the twilight’s foam  
That iron voice went wandering wide,  
And still the boy, half-fear, half-dream,  
Pressed close against his mother’s side.  

Above them burned the first white star;  
The sea breathed deep below the hill;  
And all the world seemed near and far,  
And all its terrors strangely still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Recreate Edward Thomas’s poem “The Bell,” including its imagery of a yellow flower, grasshoppers, the sea between Wales and Devon, and the mother explaining the bell in the bay.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is an original recreation inspired by Edward Thomas’s “The Bell,” using the imagery you mentioned—not the exact text of the poem:

**The Bell**

A yellow flower beside the track  
Stood bright against the summer day,  
While grasshoppers went clicking back  
Through dusty grass and heads of hay.  

Far off, beyond the fields’ green swell,  
The sea lay blue and still between  
The coasts of Wales and Devon—well  
Remembered, though but dimly seen.  

The child who heard, beneath the sky,  
A sound come faintly from the bay,  
Asked why a bell should cry and cry  
Where no church tower stood that way.  

His mother, looking to the foam  
And to the waters, deep and wide,  
Said ships had gone and not come home,  
And bells remember those who died.  

So in the bay the hidden bell  
Tolled under wave and gull and cloud,  
As if the drowned had words to tell  
But could not speak their names aloud.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Georgian-style poem in blank verse/free verse featuring a child addressing “mother,” strange brightness on a cliff, insects, sea foam like a girl’s arm, and a haunting bell heard offshore.
counterfactuals.output:
Mother, I saw a brightness on the cliff  
Where no sun fell, and no white gull had passed;  
It trembled there, as if the chalky stone  
Remembered lightning from a former world.  

The grasses whispered with their little lives;  
Thin insects, green and golden, stitched the air,  
And beetles in the thyme went armoured by  
Like knights no bigger than a baby’s thumb.  

Below, the sea came breathing in its sleep,  
And drew its foam along the shingle edge—  
So pale, so soft, it seemed a young girl’s arm  
Laid down and shining after dancing there.  

Mother, I called, but only heard the wind  
Go inland through the bracken and the wheat;  
Then far beyond the boats, beyond the haze,  
A bell began to toll beneath the sea.  

Not loud, not near, yet every stroke was clear,  
As though some drowned church lifted up its heart  
And rang for children lost before their time,  
For lamps gone out in houses by the shore.  

Mother, I was not frightened—no, not then—  
But all the insects ceased, and even the foam  
Fell back like linen folded from the dead;  
The cliff shone on, too bright for afternoon.  

I thought your hand would find my shoulder soon,  
Your voice would break the spell of stone and wave;  
But still the bell went calling from offshore,  
And still that strange light burned upon the cliff.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
